atlas.title: The map starts dark
atlas.p1: Everywhere you have not driven lies under fog. Every recorded trip burns a corridor through it, and what is left is an atlas of the roads you actually know — not a list of places you meant to visit one day.
atlas.p2: The figure under the map is the length of what is open, not the sum of your trips. The hundredth lap around your own block opens nothing, and the map is honest about that.
atlas.link: How the fog of war map works

places.title: Places, and the journeys between them
places.p1: Mark a point on a route and TripTrack starts recognising it. Return visits help you see how long the drive usually takes and which routes bring you there.
places.p2: Four trips over one long weekend are four rows in a database and one story in life. A journey is a window of dates over your own trips — the days, the kilometres and the regions counted once, in one place.

plus.title: TripTrack PRO — coming with 0.8.4
plus.p1: The next iPhone release adds an optional subscription for profile backgrounds, avatar frames and manually added trips. Version 0.8.4 is in Apple review. Recording, your diary, photos, statistics and the atlas stay free.

free.a: Recording, the diary, photos, statistics and the atlas are free. Version 0.8.4, currently in Apple review, adds optional TripTrack PRO for personalisation and manual trips.

auto.q: Does it record on its own?
auto.a: It can. Pair it with the car stereo once: recording starts when the stereo comes on and offers to finish when it goes off. Or press start yourself — while a trip is paused the app never decides on its own that it is over.

battery.a: GPS recording uses battery. Consumption depends on the phone, trip length and whether the screen and navigation are on. You can lock the screen and keep recording in the background.

account.a: You can record trips without an account. Sign in with Apple for cloud sync, social features and your own synced trips on this website. Use the same Apple Account on the iPhone and the web.

timeline.q: Is this a Google Timeline alternative?
timeline.a: TripTrack is an alternative for recording car journeys. Google Timeline still works on mobile, but no longer has a web view. TripTrack offers a drive diary on iPhone and a browser map for synced trips; it cannot import Timeline history.

atlas.q: What is the fog of war map?
atlas.a: The Atlas tab covers the world in fog and clears it along the roads you have driven. It is not a game layer laid over the map — it is the map, and the number under it is the length of what you have opened.

android.a: Not yet, and there is no date. TripTrack is written for iPhone in Apple's own frameworks by one developer; an Android version would be a second app rather than a port.

fog.h1: Fog of war map for everyday driving
fog.lead: Remember fog of war from strategy games? TripTrack covers the whole world in fog and clears it as you drive. Every kilometre is a new discovery.
fog.what_title: What is a fog of war map?
fog.what_p1: Fog of war is a video-game mechanic: the map is hidden under dark fog until you explore it. In TripTrack it works the same way — the world map starts covered, and the fog clears only where you have actually driven.
fog.what_p2: That turns every drive into a small expedition. A different route to work uncovers a new neighbourhood; a road trip cuts a whole strip out of the fog. Over time the map becomes a picture of where your life has actually taken you.
fog.what_p3: The number under the map is the length of what is open — not the sum of your trips. Your hundredth lap around your own block opens nothing, and a map that counted it would be flattering you instead of telling you something.
fog.step1_desc: On the first launch the entire map is covered. You start from nothing — like a new game.
fog.step2_desc: Every recorded trip burns a corridor through the fog. The more you drive, the more of the world is yours.
fog.step3_desc: Open the Atlas and look at the blank spots. They are the best route planner there is.
fog.step4_desc: After a recorded trip, discoveries such as passes, lighthouses, border posts and ferries leave a seal on your atlas.
fog.table_title: More than a map of where you have been

privacy.lead: TripTrack records where you drive. That is about as personal as data gets, so this page says plainly what is kept, where it is kept, and what it takes to make all of it go away.
privacy.summary_1: Trips, photos and statistics live on your iPhone. The app works with no account at all.
privacy.summary_2: With sync enabled, your library is stored on our server and can be viewed on this website after Apple sign-in. Web trip creation is not yet available.
privacy.summary_3: We don’t sell your data or use it for advertising. The services supporting sign-in, maps and the app are listed below.
privacy.phone_p1: Every trip — its track, distance, speed, elevation, photos, notes, checkpoints, places, vehicles and the atlas of what you have opened — is stored in a database inside the app on your device. Photos you attach are copied into the app's own folder. None of it is sent anywhere by default.
privacy.phone_p2: Delete a trip and it is gone from the phone. Delete the app and everything goes with it, because there is no copy elsewhere unless you made one.
privacy.cloud_title: What leaves the phone with Cloud Sync on
privacy.cloud_p1: Cloud Sync is off until you turn it on and sign in with Apple. Apple gives us a stable identifier and, if you allow it, your name and a relay e-mail address; we never see your Apple password.
privacy.cloud_p2: With it on, your trips (track, statistics, photos, checkpoints, segments), your vehicles, your journeys and your settings are uploaded so a second device can show the same library. They stay yours: other people see a trip only if you publish it, and a published trip can be unpublished.
privacy.cloud_p3: Turning Cloud Sync off stops the uploads. «Delete account» in the app erases the server copy and the phone copy in one go, and it cannot be undone.
privacy.crash_p1: The app sends crash and error reports to Sentry so that failures get fixed. Reports are scrubbed before they leave the phone: no coordinates, no trip contents, no tokens, no e-mail addresses — the stack, the app version and the device model. Our server reports its own failures the same way and scrubs them the same way: identifiers are stripped out of the request address, and the header your session token travels in is removed before anything leaves.
privacy.cookies_title: Cookies and data on this site
privacy.cookies_p1: This website sets no tracking cookies. No advertising cookies, no profiling cookies, and no third-party tracking tags. The one outside script on the whole site is Apple's, and it loads only on the sign-in page of «My trips» — it is what the Sign in with Apple button is. Our hosting provider may set a short-lived security cookie to tell a browser from a bot; that one is technical, and nothing personal can be read out of it.
privacy.cookies_p2: Visits are counted with Umami — the stock open-source build, running on our own server at analytics.trip-track.app. It is cookieless: it records the page, the referrer, the country, the browser and the screen size. Your IP address is used only to derive a daily anonymous visit id and is not stored, so a visitor cannot be followed from one day to the next. The «My trips» area is left out of the count entirely: not one address from there is sent, because the address of a trip page is the identifier of that trip.
privacy.cookies_p3: The «My trips» area keeps two things in your browser's local storage: a session token and a device id, both strictly needed to keep you signed in. They are not analytics and they are never sent anywhere but our own API. Signing out deletes the session token at once. The device id stays, deliberately: it is what makes this browser look like the same device when you sign back in, it says nothing about who you are, and clearing this site's data in your browser removes it.
privacy.cookies_p4: The map in that area draws its tiles from OpenFreeMap (tiles.openfreemap.org). Like any map provider, it sees requests for the area you are looking at. Your trips themselves are never sent there — they are drawn in your browser on top of the tiles.
privacy.cookies_p5: There are no advertising or profiling cookies on this website.
privacy.rights_p1: You can use the app with no account, delete any trip at any time, stop Cloud Sync whenever you like, unpublish anything you published, and delete the account together with everything on the server. All of it is in the app, and none of it requires writing to us first.
privacy.rights_p2: If you would rather ask a person — about what is stored, about a copy of your data, or about deleting it — write to the address below. The answer comes from the developer, because there is only one.
privacy.contact_p1: TripTrack is made by OneZee, an independent developer. Questions about this page, or about anything stored:
privacy.web_trips: You can currently view synced trips on this website. Manual creation for PRO is prepared but remains unavailable until a compatible iPhone update. When it opens, new trips will be private in your account. Drafts will stay only in the tab’s memory, so closing or reloading will discard them. Address search and road routing, when configured, send your entered address or waypoints through our server to Geoapify, without your name, email, account token or other trip history. Drawing points does not request road routing. The iPhone home privacy zone is not applied in the web editor; check route endpoints before saving.
privacy.usage_p1: From 0.8.7, Settings → Privacy → Help improve TripTrack lets you opt in to counts of recording starts, local saves and failures, Atlas opens, and save-speed buckets. UTC days of consent, delivery and the first two saved recordings, plus whether your library already had trips, help us understand first and repeat use. This is off by default, works without an account or Cloud Sync, and does not upload your trip history.
privacy.usage_p2: A fresh random code groups the counters; we store its hash without linking it to your account. No routes, coordinates, photos, notes, distance or vehicle details are included. Turning this off clears local counters and deletes server counters at the next connection. Deletion markers block delayed uploads. Inactive records and markers expire after 90 days. Re-enabling starts fresh. Uninstalling alone does not send a deletion request. This is consent-based first-party analytics, not advertising tracking; the connecting IP is still visible to server infrastructure.
